#### L3c — MFA challenge and enrollment
- Builds: `complete_mfa`, `begin_mfa_enrollment`, `confirm_mfa_enrollment`, `issue_recovery_codes` and `regenerate_recovery_codes` in `PostgresAuthenticationFlow`, using `totp_security.py`, `mfa_policy.py` and the recovery-code services that exist. Owner and Manager: a pre-authentication state until the TOTP challenge (or enrollment, for a new or reset Manager) is complete; no normal actor before that. Staff: no MFA unless the account's MFA policy is `required` (Q-156); a Staff account with MFA enrolled must complete it. Recovery codes after a first enrollment: 10 codes shown once. No SMS anywhere. The TOTP protection key comes from a protected key file at runtime (Q-155).
- Rules: DL-056, DL-058, SEC-013, SEC-071, API-096, API-098, UI-110, UI-112, DB-AUTH-003.
- Files: `auth_flow.py`, `settings.py` (a key file path setting, the path only), `.env.example` (path name only; needs the owner's yes to open it, Q-155), docs/005 notes, README run notes.
- Tests: the TEST-128 matrix (Owner and Manager blocked before MFA, Staff without MFA allowed within its capabilities, Staff with MFA must complete it; correct and wrong codes; enrollment; reuse of a TOTP code in the same step refused), TEST-129 (codes shown once, used once, regeneration invalidates the old set, wrong code counted by L3b), audit without secrets.

### 7.4 First Owner on the Mac mini (proposed runbook; built and tested in L7)

Nothing secret is ever typed on a command line, put in a file in the repository, printed to redirectable output or written to the shell history.
1. Before: all migrations are at head; no account and no bootstrap closure exist; the `prm_bootstrap` password file named in README.md (`.local/secrets/postgres_bootstrap_password`) already exists from the database setup.
2. Make the TOTP protection key without seeing it: `sudo sh -c 'umask 077; openssl rand -hex 32 > /usr/local/etc/prm/totp_protection_key'` (the path is proposed in Q-155; the file is owned by root, mode 0600; the value is never shown or typed).
3. Make a local blocklist file (common and project words such as the app name, the Property name and "password"), outside the repository.
4. Run `sudo sh scripts/bootstrap-owner.sh --username <name> --display-name "<name>" --audit-name "<name>"`. The script opens descriptor 3 with the bootstrap database URL built inside the script from the password file (shell built-ins only, so the password is never in a process list), descriptor 4 from the key file and descriptor 5 from the blocklist, then starts the command as the owner's normal user.
5. The command asks for the password on the terminal (not shown while typing; a password manager may paste it). It shows the TOTP setup key on the terminal: add it to an authenticator app already on your phone or Mac (for example the Passwords app's verification codes), then type the 6-digit code. It shows 10 recovery codes once: write them on paper and keep them in a safe place, then confirm. Everything rolls back if any step fails or the time limit passes.
6. After: clear the terminal and its scrollback (Command-K) and close the window; check with `history | tail` that only the command with names appears; sign in at the local HTTPS address with the new password and a TOTP code.
7. A second run fails closed and is audited (TEST-134); there is no web route that makes a first Owner (UI-113).

### 7.6 Risks for the whole login slice

- The app becomes reachable for the first time. Every route then depends on its own capability check; L5's inventory test is the guard that no route is left open, and it must come before any browser use with real data.
- Seeding bundles and adding `account_class` touch identity tables that the financial functions rely on (`app.assert_active_financial_actor`); both changes are additive and the financial tests must pass unchanged.
- Committed tests that build `create_app` with fakes must keep working; the new wiring is used only when a database is configured.
- Capability renames from Q-151 change committed route tests; each change is named in the report.
- The local HTTPS and key-file steps (L7) run on the owner's Mac mini; Claude Code does not read secret files and does not download anything. If a step needs a download or a package, it stops and asks.
- The build order stays: after L8 the session stops and tells the owner; the screen rebuild, slices 11 and 12 start only when the owner sends them.
